title: Autism Spectrum Condition and the Built Environment: New Perspectives on Place Attachment and Cultural Heritage
authors: John Schofield, Callum Scott, Penny Spikins & Barry Wright, 2020
central_proposition: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC) exhibit distinct patterns of engagement, place attachment, and value assignment towards the historic built environment compared to neurotypical individuals, necessitating a re-evaluation of inclusive heritage policy and practice.

concept_definitions.name: Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
concept_definitions.definition: a collection of conditions where there is impaired social behaviour, communication and language, with a narrow range of interests, preoccupations and repetitive behaviours.

concept_definitions.name: Cultural Heritage
concept_definitions.definition: heritage in contributing to people's 'ontological security', the importance of a sense of order and continuity in relation to one's lived experiences

concept_definitions.name: Aesthetics (Heritage Value)
concept_definitions.definition: ways people gain sensory and intellectual stimulation from a place

concept_definitions.name: Historical (Heritage Value)
concept_definitions.definition: ways in which people, events and aspects of life can be connected through a place to the present

concept_definitions.name: Communal (Heritage Value)
concept_definitions.definition: value derived from the meaning of a place for the people who relate to it

concept_definitions.name: Evidential (Heritage Value)
concept_definitions.definition: the potential of a place to provide evidence of past human activity

argument_structure: The paper first reviews existing literature on Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC) characteristics, focusing on social, perceptive, and behavioral differences and their influence on relationships with objects and the built environment. It then presents a large-scale survey methodology comparing individuals with ASC (AT sample) and neurotypical individuals (NT sample) on their engagement with heritage, place attachment, and valued features of buildings. The statistically significant findings from this survey are summarized, demonstrating differences in heritage engagement, values attached to buildings, attitudes towards change, and preferences for living environments. Finally, these results are discussed within the context of critical heritage studies, emphasizing the need for greater inclusivity and understanding of diverse perspectives in heritage policy and practice.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism posits that fundamental differences in brain connectivity and cognitive functioning in individuals with ASC lead to distinct ways of processing environmental information, forming attachments, and assigning value to the built environment. This includes: 1) A perceptual style drawn to detail, inanimate objects, and geometric shapes, finding comfort in their stability and certainty due to 'enhanced perceptual abilities'. 2) Difficulties with 'Theory of Mind' and empathy, leading to different social relationships and a preference for objective topics, which translates to valuing buildings more for information/structure than social connection. 3) Increased sensitivity and resistance to change, meaning alterations to the built environment can cause stress and uncertainty, especially when affecting personal significance. 4) The built environment offering a sense of security and stability (ontological security) for people with ASC, particularly when the social world is uncertain.

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Likelihood of visiting heritage sites in the last year
findings.mechanism: This may reflect a tendency to prefer solitary pursuits in individuals with autism or a lack of means of easy integration to community or accommodations for visiting heritage sites or landscape.
findings.source: Appendix B: Engagement with heritage and with the local community in general
findings.quote: AT participants were statistically less likely to have visited any heritage sites (F4,628 = 4.043, P < 0.01, see also Figure 1).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Sense of connection to the local community
findings.mechanism: Linked to difficulties understanding how other people think and feel, causing social differences and problems in everyday life.
findings.source: Appendix B: Engagement with heritage and with the local community in general
findings.quote: there was a significant negative correlation between being a member of the AT group and attachment to the community (r = -0.238, P < 0.01).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Involvement with the local community (e.g., civic or local amenity groups, clubs)
findings.mechanism: Linked to difficulties understanding how other people think and feel, causing social differences and problems in everyday life.
findings.source: Appendix B: Engagement with heritage and with the local community in general
findings.quote: 42.3% of AT participants strongly disagreed with being involved with their local community compared to 20.7% amongst the NT sample.

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Enjoyment of visiting and exploring new places
findings.mechanism: Implied preference for routine and predictability, and potential stress from novelty/uncertainty, possibly due to increased sensory abilities leading to stressful reactions to change.
findings.source: Appendix B: Engagement with heritage and with the local community in general
findings.quote: AT participants were less likely to explore new places (r = -0.271, x² = 63.86, d.f. = 4, P < 0.01).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Interest in the structure and construction of buildings
findings.mechanism: Individuals with ASC are drawn to the detail in their environments and thus an orientation towards inanimate objects and geometric shapes, linked to enhanced perceptual abilities.
findings.source: Appendix B: The value attached to different elements of buildings
findings.quote: there was a slight correlation between finding the structure and construction of buildings interesting and being in the AT group (rs = 0.087, P < 0.028).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Tendency to select extreme answers ('Not at all', 'Very much') regarding liking buildings with interesting architectural features
findings.mechanism: Implies a more categorical or less nuanced processing style, leading to strong preferences or aversions.
findings.source: Appendix B: The value attached to different elements of buildings
findings.quote: being an AT participant was significantly correlated with selecting more extreme answers ('Not at all', 'Very much') ... (rs = 0.106, P = 0.007).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Ranking of communal aspects of buildings (value derived from meaning for people who relate to it)
findings.mechanism: Linked to difficulties understanding how other people think and feel, causing social differences and a preference for objective topics.
findings.source: Appendix B: The value attached to different elements of buildings
findings.quote: participants who rank communal elements lower had a higher AQ (F3,444 = 5.183, P = 0.002, Figure 2).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Ranking of evidential features of buildings (potential to provide evidence of past human activity)
findings.mechanism: Buildings are valued as a source of interesting knowledge rather than means of social connection, aligning with a preference for objective topics and detail.
findings.source: Appendix B: The value attached to different elements of buildings
findings.quote: participants who valued the evidential basis of a building ... had a higher AQ (F3,444 = 3.670, P = 0.012, Figure 3).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Likelihood of being upset by changes to a building due to loss of historic significance
findings.mechanism: Personal attachments and a concern with change in general are more significant than wider shared social/cultural values for AT individuals, coupled with increased sensitivity and resistance to change.
findings.source: Appendix B: The evaluation of change
findings.quote: AT participants selected historical significance more than expected, AT participants selected it less than expected (rs = −0.110, P = 0.03).

findings.antecedent: Selecting personal reasons for being upset by building changes
findings.mechanism: A more personal rather than communal significance is attached to buildings by individuals with higher AQ, and it is change to this personal significance which is most upsetting.
findings.source: Appendix B: The evaluation of change
findings.quote: participants who selected personal reasons for why they were upset when a building was changed (24.2%) rather than historical reasons, were more likely to have higher AQ scores (P = 0.007).

findings.antecedent: Selecting 'other' reasons for being upset by building changes (including 'disliked change')
findings.mechanism: This reflects a general dislike and resistance to change in individuals with higher AQ.
findings.source: Appendix B: The evaluation of change
findings.quote: Participants who had 'other' reasons for why they were upset were likely to have a higher AQ score (x² = 15.589, d.f. = 4, P < 0.01, see Figure 4).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Likelihood of being pleased by drastic positive changes (renovation/demolition) to a building
findings.mechanism: General resistance to change, even if the changes are intended as positive by others.
findings.source: Appendix B: The evaluation of change
findings.quote: the AT sample was significantly less likely to be pleased by these changes (NT = 61%, AT = 49.4%, rs = −0.116, P = 0.006).

findings.antecedent: Valuing childhood favourite building for aesthetic or functional reasons
findings.mechanism: Reflects a preference for objective, structural, and functional aspects, aligning with being drawn to detail and inanimate objects.
findings.quote: participants who favoured their buildings for aesthetic and functional reasons had a much higher average AQ (30.45 ± 12.13, 32.58 ± 12.16) than those who selected historical or personal social significance as reasons (24.69 ± 12.77, 24.28 ± 12.16, P < 0.01).

findings.antecedent: Valuing current favourite building for aesthetic or functional reasons
findings.mechanism: Indicates a continued preference for objective, structural, and functional aspects into adulthood.
findings.quote: this was also found when discussing their current favourite buildings (rs = 0.167, P < 0.01), with AT participants being approximately 98% more likely to select Aesthetic or functional reasons than NT participants.

findings.antecedent: Valuing current favourite building for historical significance
findings.mechanism: Buildings are valued as a source of information/knowledge, aligning with a preference for objective topics.
findings.quote: as adults, participants who found the historical significance of a building important had a higher mean AQ (27.97 ± 12.88) and this group was now significantly different in AQ from those who chose personal social significance (P = 0.002).

findings.antecedent: Preference for a highly structured urban environment (e.g., Milton Keynes)
findings.mechanism: Certain highly ordered buildings or elements of built heritage might be particularly attractive to individuals with high AQ, aligning with a preference for predictability, geometric shapes, and low sensory uncertainty.
findings.quote: Participants who preferred to live in a highly structured built environment, being more likely to choose the town we can now identify as Milton Keynes, were likely to have a higher AQ (31.49 ± 11.40) than those choosing the less structured built environment of York (25.04 ± 11.70, P = 0.009).

findings.antecedent: Being an AT participant (high AQ score)
findings.consequent: Likelihood of spending entirely on functional aspects (100% function) for a new building
findings.mechanism: Reflects a preference for objective, practical utility over aesthetic or social considerations.
findings.quote: those in the AT (10.1%) sample were more likely to spend entirely on 'function' compared to NT participants (3.4%, x² = 15.879, d.f. = 4, P < 0.01).

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Investigate whether the observed differences in heritage engagement among individuals with ASC reflect a tendency to prefer solitary pursuits or a lack of accessible community integration/accommodations at heritage sites.
Explore how changes to buildings in general (beyond specific cases) affect individuals with high AQ, using subtly different or further questions to reveal more nuanced evidence.
Further research into why certain highly ordered buildings or elements of built heritage are particularly attractive to individuals with high AQ.
Examine whether personal significance is only important to AT individuals when a building is under threat of change or demolition, as opposed to its general value.
bridge_warrants: The theory connects ASC characteristics (social, perceptive, and behavioral differences, including 'Theory of Mind' and resistance to change) to specific patterns of engagement with the built environment and the assignment of heritage values.
It links the concept of 'ontological security' (Giddens) to the stability and comfort that the built environment can provide for people with ASC, especially when the social world is uncertain.
The framework aligns with critical heritage studies by emphasizing the importance of recognizing and accommodating diversity, difference, and equality in heritage valuation and management.

It builds upon existing research on ASC-friendly building design principles (e.g., reducing overstimulation, predictable layouts, curved walls) by extending these considerations to the historic built environment.
methodological_critiques: The paper highlights a deficiency in the current understanding of ASC perspectives within the heritage sector, noting that this understanding is needed to make heritage genuinely relevant to everyone in society.
It points out a lack of 'empirical evidence to justify current practice in the conservation of the historic environment', which this study aims to address.
limitations: It is unclear whether observed differences in heritage engagement reflect a preference for solitary pursuits in individuals with autism or a lack of means of easy integration to community or accommodations for visiting heritage sites or landscape.
The survey design might not have fully captured how changes to buildings in general (rather than specific cases) affect individuals with high AQ, suggesting a need for more nuanced questioning.
The findings regarding personal social significance for AT participants are inconclusive, requiring further research to determine if it is only important when a building is under threat.
The attractiveness of highly structured environments to individuals with high AQ warrants further exploration.
